Well, doctor, I... I suppose I came in because things have just gotten completely out of hand lately. I work down at the warehouse—been doing stocking and order filling for a good long while now, and you know, you get used to a certain rhythm. I took some college courses back in the day, so I'm no fool, but man, they just flipped everything upside down on us. 

A little while back, management decided to completely overhaul things. They changed my warehouse hours all around, and on top of that, they brought in this entirely new inventory system. Ever since they did that, I just... I feel like I’m completely falling apart. I mean, it’s not just the job, it’s my whole life right now. I’ve started missing my shifts, which isn't like me at all, I've always been a dependable worker. And it’s bleeding into the rest of my week, too. I've been skipping out on my church commitments—and I've been going there for years—but I just can't bring myself to show up or talk to anybody. 

I’m snapping at my family over the smallest little things, just biting their heads off for absolutely no reason. And the mornings... well, some mornings I just sit there on the edge of the bed, all laced up in my work boots, just staring at the floor, wondering if I can even physically bring myself to face that place anymore. I just sit there. It's just... it's all become too much to handle.

Well, doctor, that's... that's a really good question, and honestly, it's something I've been thinking about a lot lately. You see, I used to have a whole routine, a whole set of things that just made sense to me, things I looked forward to. Like, take my garden, for instance. I've always had this little vegetable patch out back. Tomatoes, peppers, a little bit of squash—nothing fancy, but I used to love getting out there in the dirt on a Saturday morning, especially before it gets too hot, you know? Just feeling the soil, watching things grow. It gave me a real sense of accomplishment, especially after being indoors at the warehouse all week under those awful fluorescent lights.

But now? Now, I just... I look out the window at it, and I see the weeds starting to creep in, and I know I should go out there, I know I used to enjoy it, but I just can't seem to muster up the energy or the... the desire. It's like the color has been drained out of everything. Even my grandkids—they used to come over on Sundays, and we'd play cards or I'd show them how to fix little things around the house. I loved those afternoons. But lately, when my daughter calls to ask if they can come by, I find myself making excuses. I tell her I'm tired, or my back is acting up, which is true sometimes, but the real reason is I just don't feel that spark anymore. I don't feel that joy. 

It's like this heavy blanket is just draped over my whole life, and everything I used to like doing just feels like another chore on a list I can't even bear to look at. I try to read the paper, something I've done every morning for forty years, and I just end up staring at the words without taking anything in. It's just... it's all so flat now. Everything is just flat.

Anxious? Well, I don't know if I'd use the word anxious, exactly. It's not like I'm sitting around biting my nails or pacing holes in the living room rug, if you know what I mean. My wife, God rest her soul, she used to get anxious about things—worrying if the stove was left on, or if the kids were going to make it home before the snow started sticking to the roads. That was anxiety. She'd get all fluttery and couldn't sit still for two minutes straight. 

But me? I don't think it's that. I mean, sure, I've got a lot on my mind with all this mess at the warehouse. Who wouldn't? When you've been doing things a certain way for so long, and then some suit in an office decides to pull the rug out from under you, it makes you think. It makes you wonder what else is going to change without anyone asking your opinion on the matter. But I wouldn't say I'm sitting around feeling on edge all day long. It's more of a... a heaviness, like I was telling you before. A real heavy feeling. 

I guess sometimes when I'm sitting on the edge of the bed in the morning, looking at those boots, my stomach might do a little bit of a flip, just dreading having to walk through those doors and figure out that new computer system they put in. The screens are so bright, and the print is so small, and they expect you to just know how to use it overnight. But I wouldn't call that being on edge most of the time. It's just the thought of the place that gets to me. Once I'm home, I just feel worn down. Just completely tapped out, you know? Not jumpy, just... done.

How long? Well, let me think back... it's been... gosh, it's got to be about five months now. Yes, five months. Because I remember exactly when it all shifted. Physical symptoms? Like my heart racing or getting all sweaty? Well, let me think about that. I know some folks get like that. My brother-in-law, Frank, he used to get the shakes so bad before he had to give a presentation at his sales job that he'd have to sit in his car for twenty minutes just doing deep breathing exercises. He'd come in and his shirt collar would be completely soaked through. But me? No, I wouldn't say I get anything like that. 

I mean, I told you about my stomach doing a little flip when I'm sitting on the edge of the bed in the morning, looking at my boots. It's just this sinking feeling, you know? Like a rock dropping right down into my gut. But it's not like my heart is pounding out of my chest or I'm breaking into a cold sweat. And I don't get the shakes. My hands are steady enough, thank the Lord, even if they are a bit arthritic these days. 

When I think about that new inventory system... well, it's more of a mental exhaustion than a physical panic. I'll be sitting in my armchair after dinner, watching the evening news, and the thought of those tiny little numbers on those bright screens will pop into my head, and I just feel... tired. Just completely drained, right down to my bones. It's like the energy just leaks right out of me. I don't start trembling or sweating or anything dramatic like that. I just feel like I'm carrying a hundred-pound sack of flour on my back, and I just want to sink into the cushions and not move.

Just feeling the soil, watching things grow. It gave me a real sense of accomplishment, especially after being indoors at the warehouse all week under those awful fluorescent lights.\n\nBut now? Now, I just... I look out the window at it, and I see the weeds starting to creep in, and I know I should go out there, I know I used to enjoy it, but I just can't seem to muster up the energy or the... the desire. It's like the color has been drained out of everything. Even my grandkids—they used to come over on Sundays, and we'd play cards or I'd show them how to fix little things around the house. I loved those afternoons. But lately, when my daughter calls to ask if they can come by, I find myself making excuses. I tell her I'm tired, or my back is acting up, which is true sometimes, but the real reason is I just don't feel that spark anymore. I don't feel that joy. \n\nIt's like this heavy blanket is just draped over my whole life, and everything I used to like doing just feels like another chore on a list I can't even bear to look at. I try to read the paper, something I've done every morning for forty years, and I just end up staring at the words without taking anything in. It's just... it's all so flat now. Everything is just flat.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel anxious or on edge most of the time?\n\nPatient: Anxious? Well, I don't know if I'd use the word anxious, exactly. It's not like I'm sitting around biting my nails or pacing holes in the living room rug, if you know what I mean. My wife, God rest her soul, she used to get anxious about things—worrying if the stove was left on, or if the kids were going to make it home before the snow started sticking to the roads. That was anxiety. She'd get all fluttery and couldn't sit still for two minutes straight. \n\nBut me? I don't think it's that. I mean, sure, I've got a lot on my mind with all this mess at the warehouse. Who wouldn't? When you've been doing things a certain way for so long, and then some suit in an office decides to pull the rug out from under you, it makes you think. It makes you wonder what else is going to change without anyone asking your opinion on the matter. But I wouldn't say I'm sitting around feeling on edge all day long. It's more of a... a heaviness, like I was telling you before. A real heavy feeling. \n\nI guess sometimes when I'm sitting on the edge of the bed in the morning, looking at those boots, my stomach might do a little bit of a flip, just dreading having to walk through those doors and figure out that new computer system they put in. The screens are so bright, and the print is so small, and they expect you to just know how to use it overnight. But I wouldn't call that being on edge most of the time. It's just the thought of the place that gets to me. Once I'm home, I just feel worn down. Just completely tapped out, you know? Not jumpy, just... done.\n\nDoctor: Have you had any thoughts of not wanting to be alive or wishing you could just go to sleep and not wake up?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, that's... that's a heavy question. A very heavy question. And I appreciate you asking it, I really do, because I know people my age, sometimes we don't like to talk about those sorts of things. My buddy Al, he passed a few years back, and he never would have admitted to feeling down, not for a second. But me... well, I try to be honest. And honestly? No. No, I haven't had any thoughts like that. \n\nI mean, don't get me wrong, I'm miserable. I told you about how flat everything feels, how I just sit there looking at my boots in the morning. It's a terrible feeling, just this awful weight pressing down on me, making every little thing feel like moving a mountain. And sleep... well, sleep is an escape, isn't it? When I finally do manage to drift off, after tossing and turning and thinking about those new warehouse schedules and all those blinking lights on the inventory scanners... sleep is a relief. It's the only time I'm not feeling this... this crushing sense of being overwhelmed by it all. \n\nBut wanting to not wake up? No. No, I don't want that. I just want things to go back to how they were. I want to wake up and feel like tending to my tomatoes. I want to wake up and feel like calling my daughter to see the grandkids. I want to wake up and go to work and know what I'm doing and feel like I'm contributing something, instead of feeling like I'm drowning in a puddle. I just want my life back, doctor. I don't want it to end. I just want the life I had before all this mess started. So, no, I haven't had any thoughts of wanting to be dead. Just... just thoughts of wanting things to be different. Better. Like they used to be.\n\nDoctor: How long have you been feeling this way?\n\nPatient: How long? Well, let me think back... it's been... gosh, it's got to be about five months now. Yes, five months. Because I remember exactly when it all shifted. It was right around the time they brought in those new folks from corporate. Before that, I had my routine, you know? Just completely threw the old shifts out the window without so much as a 'by your leave' to the guys who've been working the floor for years. Five months of looking at my boots in the morning and dreading having to lace them up. Like my heart racing or getting all sweaty? Well, let me think about that. I know some folks get like that. He'd come in and his shirt collar would be completely soaked through. But me? No, I wouldn't say I get anything like that. \n\nI mean, I told you about my stomach doing a little flip when I'm sitting on the edge of the bed in the morning, looking at my boots. It's just this sinking feeling, you know? Like a rock dropping right down into my gut. But it's not like my heart is pounding out of my chest or I'm breaking into a cold sweat. And I don't get the shakes. My hands are steady enough, thank the Lord, even if they are a bit arthritic these days. \n\nWhen I think about that new inventory system... well, it's more of a mental exhaustion than a physical panic. I'll be sitting in my armchair after dinner, watching the evening news, and the thought of those tiny little numbers on those bright screens will pop into my head, and I just feel... tired. Just completely drained, right down to my bones. It's like the energy just leaks right out of me. I don't start trembling or sweating or anything dramatic like that. I just feel like I'm carrying a hundred-pound sack of flour on my back, and I just want to sink into the cushions and not move. \n\nSo, no, I don't really have those kinds of physical reactions. No racing heart, no sweating, no trembling. Just that heavy, tired feeling, and maybe that little stomach flip in the mornings. It's not a panic, doctor. It's just... it's just this awful, heavy dread.\n\nDoctor: Have you been avoiding certain tasks or situations outside of work because they remind you of the problems you're having at the warehouse?\n\nPatient: Avoiding things outside of work because they remind me of the warehouse? Guilty? Worthless? Well... no. No, I wouldn't say that at all, doctor. I mean, why on earth should I feel guilty? I've been working hard my entire life. Blame myself? Oh, heaven's no. Why would I blame myself? Like I said, I've been doing this job, and doing it well, for a very long time. I mean, think about it from my perspective. Lost interest? No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. I mean, if you're asking if I just don't care about the things I love anymore, that's definitely not it. 

Like I mentioned a minute ago about the yard—I haven't gotten the mower out the last couple of weekends, sure, but it's not because I don't want to or because I don't care. I've got this beautiful old oak rocking chair I picked up at a flea market over in the next county back in... well, it must have been early spring before all this nonsense at work started. I was making great progress on it, too. I'm just too exhausted and down to do much of anything else.\n\nDoctor: Have you lost a significant amount of weight over the past five months?\n\nPatient: Weight? No, no, I wouldn't say that. I haven't noticed any real change there. You see, I've been wearing the same size 36 waist work trousers—the heavy-duty canvas ones, you know, because the regular denim just wears right out at the knees when you're dealing with the lower pallets all day—for, gosh, it must be going on ten or twelve years now. And they still fit exactly the same. I check my belt notch every morning when I'm putting those boots on. It's the third hole from the end, same as it always is. \n\nEven with all this... this heaviness I was telling you about, and being so tired all the time, my stomach still expects to be fed. I still have my bowl of oatmeal every single morning, though I'll admit I haven't been putting the fresh sliced bananas on it like I used to, because I'm just too drained to bother going to the store to keep them stocked. And in the evenings, when I'm sitting in that armchair I mentioned, watching the news and trying not to think about work, sometimes I find myself just mindlessly eating a handful of salted peanuts or a couple of those oatmeal raisin cookies from the tin. It's not even because I'm really hungry, it's just... well, it's just something to do with my hands while I'm sitting there feeling so weighed down. \n\nSo, no, the scale hasn't really budged at all. I stepped on it just last week in the bathroom—I have one of those old mechanical dial ones, not the digital kind, I don't trust the digital ones to last—and the needle was hovering right around 185. Which is exactly where it was five months ago, before all this corporate nonsense started. So no, I haven't lost a significant amount of weight. I'm carrying the exact same amount of weight on my frame, it just... it just feels a whole lot heavier to carry around these days, if you know what I mean.\n\nDoctor: Do you often feel guilty or worthless about your situation at work or your inability to cope with the changes?\n\nPatient: Guilty? I did a little bit of college right out of high school, you know, but I realized pretty quick I'm a man who likes to be on his feet, getting things done, moving things around, not just sitting behind a desk listening to lectures. I’ve been a stocker and order filler for decades. I know that warehouse like the back of my own hand. If you hand me a traditional paper manifest, I can pull a pallet together faster and more accurately than any of these twenty-something kids they hire nowadays. I know exactly where everything is, from the heavy industrial solvents in aisle twelve right down to the seasonal overstock in the back corner. \n\nSo, worthless? Absolutely not. I know the value of an honest day's work, and I've given them more than my fair share of those over the years. It’s not a failing on my part that I'm struggling so much with these changes. It’s the changes themselves! Some corporate bigwig in an air-conditioned office, probably three states away, decides we all need to use these tiny little digital scanners with screens so bright they give you a headache and buttons the size of a pinhead. And suddenly the way I've done my job perfectly well for years isn't good enough anymore. It’s just ridiculous. \n\nI don't feel guilty that my hands—which have a touch of arthritis, as I mentioned—don't want to punch in a twelve-digit barcode just to move a simple box of motor oil from the receiving dock to shelf B. I feel... well, I feel frustrated by it, and mostly I just feel that bone-deep exhaustion I was telling you about. It’s the sheer nonsense of it all that drains the life right out of me. But I certainly don't sit in my armchair in the evenings thinking I'm a worthless person. I know exactly what I'm worth, doctor. It's just a crying shame the company doesn't seem to value it anymore, just because I don't speak the same language as their new computer system. So, no, no guilt. No feeling worthless. Just that heavy, awful dread about having to go back in tomorrow and fight with those machines all over again.\n\nDoctor: Do you often blame yourself for not being able to adapt to the changes at work?\n\nPatient: Blame myself? Oh, heaven's no. Why would I blame myself? Like I said, I've been doing this job, and doing it well, for a very long time. I mean, think about it from my perspective. I'm seventy-four years old. I've spent my whole life working with my hands, moving actual, physical things. I know how to read a manifest, I know how to stack a pallet so it doesn't tip when the forklift takes a corner too sharp—which, let me tell you, happens more often than management wants to admit with some of the younger drivers they hire. \n\nI know the physical reality of the job. So when they come in and say, \"Okay, forget all that, now you have to stare at this little glowing rectangle and tap these tiny little buttons every time you move a single box,\" well, how is it my fault that my brain and my hands don't want to work that way? It's not a character flaw that I can't just flip a switch and become a computer expert overnight. \n\nI mean, I look at these young kids they bring in, they're walking around with their faces buried in their phones all day anyway, so of course tapping on a scanner comes naturally to them. But they don't know the first thing about warehouse logistics! They don't know that the heavy-duty industrial cleaner needs to be stored on the bottom rack because if a bottle leaks, it'll eat right through the cardboard of the paper goods stored underneath it. I know that. I've learned that through years of experience. \n\nBut does the scanner know that? Does the computer system care? No. It just wants you to scan the barcode and put it in slot 42-B, regardless of what makes sense. So, no, I don't sit around blaming myself. I blame the people who decided to fix something that wasn't broken. I blame the system that treats a man with decades of practical knowledge like he's obsolete just because his thumbs aren't fast enough on a touchscreen. It's not my fault they changed the rules of the game in the fourth quarter. And the grandkids, well, they're just being kids, running around the living room and making noise like kids do, but lately the sound of it just sets my teeth on edge and I end up barking at them to quiet down. It’s terrible, it really is. I'm just so wound up and drained all at once, even on my days off. \n\nAnd it's not just the temper, doctor. It's... it's affecting everything I do. I'm actually missing shifts at the warehouse now, which is something I never, ever used to do. I've always prided myself on my attendance. But now? I'm even missing my church commitments. I've been helping set up the folding chairs and tables for the Sunday school rooms for I don't know how many years—fifteen, maybe twenty?—and lately I just haven't been showing up for it. I just can't bring myself to leave the house. \n\nSome mornings, it's a struggle just to get out the door. I'll get up, do my routine, have my bowl of oatmeal, and I'll sit down in the hallway to lace up my boots... and I just sit there. I'll just sit there in my work boots for twenty, thirty minutes, staring at the floorboards, just wondering if I can even face the place anymore. The thought of going in and dealing with those scanners and the new schedule... it just paralyzes me. So, yes, the short temper is definitely there, but it's really just a part of this whole... this whole falling apart that's been happening to me lately.\n\nDoctor: Do you often feel like you're a burden to others or that you're worthless as a person?\n\nPatient: Well, like I was saying just a little bit ago about the work situation, doctor, I certainly don't feel worthless. And a burden? No, no, I really wouldn't say that either. I mean, my whole life, I've been the one carrying the load, not the other way around. I've always been the provider. Ever since my kids were little—and they're all grown up now, of course, with houses and kids of their own—I made sure there was food on the table, bills were paid on time, and everything was taken care of. \n\nEven now, with my wife, I'm the one who does the heavy lifting around the house. I mean, sure, I might be sitting in the hallway staring at my work boots some mornings, like I just told you, and I know I’ve been snapping at everyone, which I truly hate... but I'm not a burden to them. They know who I am. They know I've worked my fingers to the bone for this family for fifty years. \n\nIt's just this whole mess at the warehouse that's got me tied up in knots. I'm a husband, a grandfather, a hard worker. So, no, I don't feel like a burden, and I definitely know my worth. I still care very much about how my property looks. Lost interest? No, I wouldn't say that. I really wouldn't. It's not that the interest is gone at all. 

Take my yard, for instance. I've always taken immense pride in my property. I have this old riding mower, bought it back in the late nineties, and I still maintain the engine myself. I still care about it. I look out the front window and I see the edging along the driveway getting a little messy, or the grass getting too high around the base of the big oak tree out front, and it bothers me. It really does. I still get my seed catalogs in the mail, and I sit there at the kitchen table with my reading glasses on, looking through them, planning out what I'd *like* to do. Appetite? Well, let me think on that for a second... No, I wouldn't say my appetite has changed. Not the actual desire for food, anyway. 

I mean, the *schedule* of when I eat is completely turned upside down, just like everything else I've been telling you about. It used to be I had my routine, you know? I’d wake up, have a bowl of oatmeal at 5:00 AM, head to the warehouse, and then at exactly 10:30 AM I’d be in the breakroom with my lunch cooler. I'd sit in the exact same chair, have a turkey sandwich, maybe an apple, and a thermos of black coffee. Every single day, regular as a metronome. 

But now, with these crazy swing shifts and late nights, half the time I’m eating what you’d call 'dinner' at three in the afternoon, or I'm sitting on a stack of pallets at midnight trying to choke down a cold sandwich while those efficiency kids are running around shouting about the new routing protocols. It completely throws off your whole system, eating at those odd hours under those buzzing fluorescent lights. 

But as far as the appetite itself goes? No, I'm still eating about the same amount. I have to, really. I'm burning so much physical and mental energy just trying to keep up, dragging my feet across that concrete floor, dealing with all the misplaced shipments... if I didn't eat, I'd probably just keel over right there in the loading bay. Food is just fuel for the engine, and the engine is working absolute overtime right now. So I still get hungry, I still finish whatever I pack for my shift, and I haven't noticed myself eating any more or any less than I did before all this nonsense started.

Weight? No, no, I haven't lost any weight. Not a pound, as far as I can tell.
